title: the sounds
hook: a drum at the end of a dance, and the list of sounds that tradition says fell out of it
tomorrow: Krishna's name has no i in Sanskrit. so where did the i go?

segments.voice: These days belong to the sounds: Sanskrit taken in by the ear before the eye. Today, a story about where the list of those sounds came from. It starts with a drum.

Plenty of songs start with a drummer clicking the sticks: one, two, three, four, and the whole band knows where to come in. Here's an old story with a count-in of its own. Shiva, as Nataraja, the lord of dance, is finishing his dance. Sages stand around him, waiting for something they can't name yet. As the dance ends, he lifts his small drum and strikes it. Again. Again. The verse that tells this even counts the beats: nine times, and five times. And each beat comes out as a cluster of sounds. What are they for?
screen: `ONE, TWO, THREE, FOUR.` → `SHIVA FINISHES HIS DANCE.` → `NINE BEATS, AND FIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's what the beats were, as tradition tells it. Short strings of letters. A, i, u, with a marker at the end. Then the vowels that come after. Then e and o. On through the consonants, to the very last one, ha. They're called the Shiva Sutras, the threads of Shiva, and they sit at the head of Panini's grammar. Tradition says Panini himself received them from the drum. Now the clever part, and this part is in the grammar itself. The lists aren't the alphabet in its usual order. They're grouped so a rule can name a whole set of sounds in one short word. Take the first sound of one list and the marker at the end of a later one, and you've named everything between. Ac, said uch, means every vowel. Hal means every consonant. So when a rule needs to say before a vowel, it takes a single word: aci. A drumbeat became a shorthand. And the story keeps its order on purpose. The sages around Shiva didn't get a book. They got a rhythm, and had to listen. Sound first, heard and repeated. Then the rule that explains what was heard.
screen: `STRINGS OF SOUNDS, OFF THE DRUM.` · `THE SHIVA SUTRAS, AT THE HEAD OF PANINI.` · `AC: EVERY VOWEL IN ONE WORD.` · `THEY GOT A RHYTHM, NOT A BOOK.` · then, large: `SOUND FIRST. THEN THE RULE.`

segments.voice: Tap a slow beat with one finger, on a table or your knee, and listen only to that sound: where it starts, how it fades. Let the taps space out until there's more silence than sound. Then stop, and listen to the quiet the last one leaves.
The sounds: today, the lists tradition says came off Shiva's drum, the Shiva Sutras. Sound first, and the rule after.
Something to keep: before any rule in the grammar, there were the sounds, heard and repeated. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Students of Panini's grammar learn the Shiva Sutras by heart, usually by reciting them aloud, and the story of Shiva's drum is told as the origin of the list.

Written fresh in v3. Days 1439-1442 ('the sounds') were not on disk when this was written, so the angle (Shiva's drum and the Shiva Sutras) could not be checked against them; please make sure it doesn't repeat one of those days.

The drum story: Nandikeshvara's Kashika, opening verse (nrittavasane natarajarajo nanada dhakkam navapanchavaram...). The 'nine and five times' count is the verse's own. The tradition that Panini received the sutras from the drum is popular tradition; the script says 'tradition says'. Confirm.
ac (a ... c in 'ai au c') = all vowels; hal (ha ... l, the last sutra) = all consonants; Ashtadhyayi 1.1.71 for how the abbreviations work. Confirm the plain-English description.

Priya storyline (days 1443-1456): she says yes to reading one Sanskrit line at her school's senior send-off; Nani picks the line (vasudhaiva kutumbakam, introduced day 1446), she learns its sounds and joins, and says it on day 1456. The previous writer's Priya thread (days 1429-1442) was not on disk; this opening doesn't depend on it.
Surprising fact: one short word, ac, names every Sanskrit vowel in Panini's grammar.
